t: Section 723(e) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000 (Public Law 106–65; 113 Stat. 697) is amended by striking paragraphs (1) through (4) and inserting the following:“(1) Measures of the quality of health care furnished, including timeliness and accessibility of care.“(2) Population health.“(3) Patient safety.“(4) Patient satisfaction.“(5) The extent of use of evidence-based health care practices.“(6) The effectiveness of biosurveillance in detecting an emerging epidemic.”.

fable.w: The section only replaces a list of subject-matter items (quality of care, population health, patient safety, patient satisfaction, and so on) in an existing provision of the FY2000 NDAA. The tempting reading is that "patient satisfaction" or "accessibility of care" implies public input, but these are topics to be covered, not a process for consulting anyone outside the federal government. The text contains no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, outside consultation, or right to sue.

qwen_block.w: This section merely lists metrics for evaluating health care quality (e.g., patient satisfaction, safety). It does not establish a process for outside parties to consult with, advise, or participate in federal decision-making. There is no mention of public comment periods, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states or tribes.
qwen_block.s: Section 723(e) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000 (Public Law 106–65; 113 Stat. 697) is amended by striking paragraphs (1) through (4) and inserting the following:“(1) Measures of the quality of health care furnished, including timeliness and accessibility of care.“(2) Population health.“(3) Patient safety.“(4) Patient satisfaction.“(5) The extent of use of evidence-based health care practices.“(6) The effectiveness of biosurveillance in detecting an emerging epidemic.”.

opus.w: The section only amends a list of subjects: quality of care, population health, patient safety, patient satisfaction, use of evidence-based practices and biosurveillance effectiveness. It sets up no comment period, hearing, outside advisory body, consultation with outside groups or right to sue. Seeing 'patient satisfaction' as a measure is not the same as patients taking part in a federal decision, so nothing here brings outsiders into the government's decision.
opus.b: 1. **Reasoning.** The tempting reading is that changing a list of health-care measures in a defense law involves an outside process. Nothing in the text supports that. The amendment only replaces paragraphs (1) through (4) with a list of six topics, such as quality of care, patient safety and biosurveillance. It does not mention a comment period, hearing, advisory panel with outside members, consultation with states or tribes, or a right to sue. Any council that section 723 sets up is not described here. Even if it were, it may be made up only of federal officials, which would not count.
